items.stem: A returns-processing agent holds five role-scoped tools used in one refund decision: lookup, return-window check, fraud flag, refund issuance, and credit application. Ahead of peak volume, a reviewer proposes splitting it into eligibility and execution agents for Finance. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Split into eligibility and execution agents, adding a shared correlation ID so both calls trace to one refund request.
Split into a role-scoped eligibility agent and a role-scoped execution agent, as the reviewer proposes.
Remove the fraud-flag tool so the agent holds four tools instead of five, avoiding the need to split at all.
Keep the tools in one agent; splitting would separate return-window check from refund issuance, risking stale eligibility.

items.whyRight: The five tools already form one role-scoped decision, well inside the range scoping is meant to produce. Splitting the return-window check from refund issuance forces two separate turns, letting the eligibility window close or reopen before the refund it authorized actually posts.

whyWrong.A: A shared correlation ID makes the split traceable end to end but does not stop the return-window check and the refund decision from landing in separate turns.
whyWrong.B: This is the answer for an oversized, multi-role tool surface; splitting a genuinely small, single-decision set of five tools adds a hop this scenario never needed.
whyWrong.C: Fraud review is a needed capability the workflow uses, not the cause of the split proposal; removing it sidesteps the question instead of answering it.

items.t1Clause: the agent already holds only five role-scoped tools used together in one refund decision
items.factAnswerRaw: Keep the tools in one agent; splitting would separate return-window check from refund issuance, risking stale eligibility.

items.stem: An agent's toolset includes a bulk-export capability no current workflow calls. Security proposes logging every export call and reviewing it monthly, calling this least privilege in practice, ahead of a regulator's access-minimization audit next quarter. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Remove the bulk-export capability from the tool set; no workflow needs it, so logging only compensates.
Keep the capability, and log every export call for the regulator's review.
Keep the capability, but restrict export calls to a limited weekly time window.
Keep the capability, but require a manager's confirmation before each export call.

items.whyRight: Least privilege means the permission does not exist, not that it exists under watch. Since no workflow calls bulk-export, removing it closes the gap outright; logging, time-boxing, and confirmation are controls for privileges the team has actively decided to keep, which this one is not.

whyWrong.B: Logging records that the export happened after the fact; it never stops an unneeded capability from being used, and the regulator wants access minimized, not narrated.
whyWrong.C: A time window narrows when the unneeded export can run, not whether it should exist at all, leaving the capability available every week.
whyWrong.D: Manager confirmation gates a use the workflow was never meant to have; a legitimate need is what confirmation is for, and this capability has none.

items.t1Clause: no current workflow calls the bulk-export capability

items.stem: A support-triage system sits at its 3-second p95 SLA with no slack, three accuracy points short of target. Static preamble is resent uncached on every call, and a redundant retrieval hop duplicates one lookup. A reranking pass would add 300ms. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Add the reranking pass and quietly extend the SLA to 3.3 seconds without consulting the business.
Cut the number of retrieved chunks to make room for the reranking pass inside budget.
Add the reranking pass now, and monitor p95 latency weekly to catch any SLA breach.
Fix the caching and the redundant hop first; only then decide whether the reranking pass fits inside the recovered budget.

items.whyRight: No slack exists, so any added stage risks the SLA outright. The uncached preamble and the duplicate hop are wasted latency already in the pipeline; recovering that budget through restructuring costs no accuracy, unlike cutting context or breaching the SLA for a reranking pass.

whyWrong.A: Extending the SLA without the business's sign-off breaches a stated commitment to buy accuracy nobody authorized, at a system already out of slack.
whyWrong.B: Cutting retrieved context removes a working mechanism and typically loses more accuracy than the reranking pass would return, the opposite of the goal.
whyWrong.C: Weekly monitoring reports a breach after it happens; it does not stop the reranking pass from pushing an already zero-slack system over budget.

items.t1Clause: no slack exists in the latency budget
items.factAnswerRaw: Look for wasted latency (ordering, caching, redundant hops) before cutting retrieved context

items.stem: Per policy, an observability system inherits the sensitivity of what it captures. A clinical-support agent's tracing plan logs full patient records to a store every engineer can query, deferring redaction and retention ahead of a compliance audit. What should the architect require?

opts.t: Encrypt the trace store at rest and require engineers to sign in through single sign-on.
Add per-stage timing to the tracing plan, and ship the store without other changes.
Design redaction, retention limits, and access control for the trace store now, alongside the tracing pipeline itself.
Pause tracing entirely until legal signs off on a full data-handling policy for the store.

items.whyRight: The trace store now holds full patient records, so it inherits their sensitivity the moment it exists. Redaction, retention limits and access control belong on the pipeline's launch date, not a later phase, because deferring them leaves regulated data exposed to every engineer with query access.

whyWrong.A: Encryption and single sign-on protect the store from outside attackers but do nothing about every engineer's standing entitlement to query patient records inside it.
whyWrong.B: Per-stage timing helps diagnose a latency regression, not a data-sensitivity gap; patient records still sit in a store with no redaction or scoped access.
whyWrong.D: Pausing tracing removes a working diagnostic capability the team needs, rather than scoping the store's sensitivity the way the principle actually requires.

items.t1Clause: the tracing plan logs full patient records, i.e. the traces will contain regulated content
items.factAnswerRaw: Design redaction, retention and access control on the trace store at the same time as the pipeline

items.stem: A helpdesk knowledge base holds support threads of 3 to 40 messages, chunked message by message across 50,000 tickets a month. Retrieved chunks are often a lone reply with no problem statement, missing a 2-minute response SLA. What should the architect change?

opts.t: Apply fixed 512-token windows with 50-token overlap across every ticket thread instead.
Build a classifier that routes each message to whichever adjacent messages it depends on before embedding.
Re-chunk each thread as one whole-ticket chunk instead of one chunk per message, keeping the full exchange together.
Keep per-message chunking, and prepend the ticket's subject line to every message before embedding.

items.whyRight: A ticket's replies only make sense against the problem statement above them, so the ticket, not the message, is the unit that stands alone. Whole-thread chunks preserve that at any thread length up to 40 messages, without touching embedding size.

whyWrong.A: Fixed windows change how much text sits in a chunk, not where the boundary falls; a 512-token cut can still isolate a reply from its problem statement.
whyWrong.B: A dependency classifier is a new component with its own failure mode, built to solve a boundary problem that a per-ticket chunk already solves outright.
whyWrong.D: A subject line tells the model what the ticket is about but still leaves each reply's chunk missing the specific problem it was answering.

items.t1Clause: the knowledge base holds structured support threads of 3 to 40 messages
items.factAnswerRaw: Chunk per ticket, not per message

items.stem: A field-service knowledge base mixes troubleshooting prose with inline part numbers, and 500 technicians query it using both plain descriptions and exact part numbers. Dense-only retrieval returns a 30% hit rate on part-number searches, a safety concern on critical equipment. What should the architect implement?

opts.t: Build a knowledge graph over the equipment hierarchy to resolve part-number lookups.
Replace dense retrieval with lexical-only search, since technicians mainly need exact part-number matches.
Keep dense-only retrieval, and have technicians manually check the part number in the parts catalog.
Add lexical retrieval alongside dense search and fuse the rankings for both query types.

items.whyRight: The corpus mixes prose and identifiers, and technicians query both ways, which is exactly the condition hybrid retrieval exists for. Fusing lexical and dense rankings recovers exact part-number matches without sacrificing the paraphrase tolerance plain-language descriptions still need.

whyWrong.A: A knowledge graph answers relationship questions like what superseded a part, not the exact-match problem a part-number search actually has here.
whyWrong.B: Technicians query both ways, by the scenario's own account; dropping dense retrieval would break every plain-language, paraphrased search that is not identifier-based.
whyWrong.C: Manual catalog lookup patches the miss after retrieval has already failed, and adds a step for every technician instead of fixing the search itself.

items.t1Clause: technicians query the corpus using both plain descriptions and exact part numbers

notes: g23 (F-3.6-04): T1 resolution is softer than the batch's other items. Section 3.6's decision table keys this row on a single trigger condition (traces will contain regulated content) rather than a contrasting pair; t1Clause inverts that trigger (no regulated content reaches the trace) and t1Alt=A assumes standard security hygiene becomes adequate once the row-4 mandate no longer applies, which is a reasonable inference rather than a row stated outright. Not IRREDUCIBLE -- the item's own correctness and its T2/T3/T4 pass cleanly -- but worth the grounding audit's confirmation on T1 specifically.
